summary: Describes Core Based Trees, a design for multicast routing that builds one delivery tree for each group, shared by all senders and receivers. This differs from schemes that build a separate tree per sender. It was published as an experimental protocol and is now historic.

eli5.summary: Instead of drawing a separate road map for every person sending a message to a group, everyone shares one big tree of roads. It uses fewer roads but can be longer trips.

subtitle: Shared-tree multicast routing architecture with O(G) scaling.

tldr.problem: Early multicast routing built a separate delivery tree for every sender in every group (source-based trees), scaling as O(S*G) where S is the number of senders and G is the number of groups. This approach consumes too much router state for large-scale deployment, particularly when many senders exist in a group.
tldr.mechanism: CBT uses a single shared tree per group rooted at a core router, shared by all senders and receivers. All senders send to the core and all receivers join the tree at the core, reducing state growth to O(G) regardless of the number of senders per group.
tldr.outcome: CBT was published as Experimental in 1997 and is now Historic. While the shared-tree architecture proved influential on later protocols such as PIM Sparse Mode, CBT itself did not achieve wide deployment. The scalability advantages remain important for understanding multicast routing design trade-offs.

today: RFC 2201 is Historic. The CBT multicast routing architecture was published in September 1997 as an Experimental protocol and did not achieve widespread deployment. However, the paper's analysis of scaling characteristics proved influential: later protocols such as PIM Sparse Mode adopted the shared-tree approach with a rendezvous point, incorporating CBT's scalability insights. Today, CBT remains valuable as a pedagogical reference for understanding multicast routing fundamentals and the fundamental trade-offs between source-based and shared-tree designs.

sections.title: The Problem with Source-Based Trees
sections.content:
RFC 2201 describes the architecture of Core Based Trees (CBT), a multicast routing approach designed to address fundamental scaling limitations in earlier multicast protocols. Early multicast algorithms, including those by Deering in the late 1980s, built a separate multicast distribution tree for each source (or source subnetwork) in every group. This means a group with 100 sources and 1,000 other groups in the network could generate 100,000 distinct trees in the routers.

The problem becomes more severe when considering real-world multicast applications. While some applications (like video lectures) have one or a few senders, others like distributed interactive simulation or multiplayer gaming have many active senders, often with many of those senders also being receivers. As the MBONE expanded in the 1990s and predictions suggested thousands of multicast groups would eventually exist simultaneously, router state maintenance became the dominant scaling factor. Source-based approaches scale as O(S*G) (state grows with the number of sources times the number of groups), which limits growth to thousands of active groups.
sections.eli5: In old multicast, if a group had 100 people sending, the network had to keep track of 100 separate trees for that group alone. With thousands of groups, that meant millions of trees to track, and routers ran out of memory. CBT fixes this by using just one tree per group.

sections.title: Source Trees: Distance-Vector and Link-State Algorithms
sections.content:
Source-based multicast algorithms come in two main varieties. Distance-vector multicast (used by DVMRP) uses a reverse-path forwarding technique: a packet is forwarded only if it arrives on the interface that would be used to reach the source. This is a "broadcast and prune" approach where packets are initially flooded, and routers send pruning messages back toward the source if they have no group members. However, this approach requires state (prune information) at many routers that do not lead to members, wasting resources on wide-area networks where group members are sparsely distributed.

Link-state multicast (like M-OSPF) has every router compute the shortest-path tree for every source-group pair. The advantage is efficient trees—each packet only traverses routers that lead to members. However, the disadvantage is severe: routers must flood group membership information throughout the domain, and each router must run expensive Dijkstra calculations for each active source. This does not scale for wide-area multicast.

Both approaches share a fundamental limitation: they generate tree state proportional to the number of senders. The RFC argues that this O(S*G) scaling is unacceptable for large-scale deployment.
sections.eli5: Distance-vector sends packets everywhere and prunes back where there are no members—lots of wasted effort. Link-state makes perfect trees but every router must calculate a tree for every sender, which is slow. Both multiply the number of trees by the number of senders, which becomes a nightmare.

sections.title: The Shared-Tree Solution
sections.content:
CBT solves the scaling problem by building a single shared tree per group, rooted at a designated core router (also called a rendezvous point). All senders and receivers use the same tree, shared across the group. The key insight is that state now scales as O(G)—linear in the number of groups, independent of the number of senders. A network with 1,000 groups and 1,000 senders per group still maintains only 1,000 tree entries (one per group), not 1,000,000.

The shared tree has two immediate benefits. First, routers only maintain state for networks and links that lead to interested receivers—no state exists for paths between non-member senders and the core. Second, a sender not yet on the tree simply sends its data to the core router (via IP-in-IP encapsulation), avoiding the need for intermediate routers to know about the multicast group. The core decapsulates and disseminates the packet down the tree.

The RFC includes a comparison table showing that CBT scales dramatically better than DVMRP: with 1,000 groups and varying numbers of senders per group, DVMRP requires 6,000 to 60,000 router entries, while CBT requires only 1,000 entries regardless of sender count. This scaling advantage is the primary motivation for the shared-tree architecture.
sections.eli5: CBT uses one tree per group. All senders and receivers use the same tree, meeting at the core. This means you only need one tree per group, not one per sender. A network with 1,000 groups keeps 1,000 trees, not millions. That saves enormous amounts of router memory.

sections.title: Design Requirements and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The CBT architecture was designed with four key requirements in mind. Scalability was the paramount goal: the designers deliberately chose to maintain O(G) scaling even though it might mean longer paths for some packets. Unlike PIM Sparse Mode (which attempts to switch to shortest-path trees), CBT accepts some delay in exchange for vastly better state scaling. Robustness required mechanisms to handle the shared tree's single point of failure: the core router. If the core fails, the tree breaks, so CBT must detect this quickly and failover to a replacement core. Simplicity was valued—CBT is simpler than most other multicast protocols, which can lead to better performance. Finally, interoperability was essential, since the Internet is heterogeneous; CBT was designed with mechanisms to interoperate with DVMRP and other protocols.

The architecture makes a deliberate trade-off: shared trees may result in longer paths than shortest-path trees, since all traffic is routed through the core rather than directly from source to receiver. However, this delay is acceptable for most applications, and in some cases can be minimized by placing the core router in the locality of typical senders. The RFC argues that the memory savings justify this trade-off, especially as multicast deployment grows.
sections.eli5: CBT prioritizes memory over path length. It accepts that packets might take a longer path (through the core) in exchange for using far less router memory. For most applications, this is a good trade-off. The protocol is also designed to handle core failures and work with other multicast protocols on the Internet.

sections.title: Influence and Historical Status
sections.content:
RFC 2201 was published in September 1997 as the architectural foundation for CBT version 2 (RFC 2189). The paper's analysis of scaling characteristics was influential in the multicast routing community, and the shared-tree architecture influenced the design of later protocols, most notably PIM Sparse Mode, which also uses a core (called a Rendezvous Point) but adds mechanisms to switch to shortest-path trees for efficiency.

CBT itself, however, did not see significant deployment. By the time CBT reached experimental status, PIM Sparse Mode and other approaches were already becoming more popular. CBT is now Historic; it remains pedagogically important for understanding multicast routing fundamentals and the trade-offs between source-based and shared-tree approaches. The scaling analysis and design rationale in this RFC have proven enduring, and the O(G) versus O(S*G) distinction remains central to multicast routing discussions today.
sections.eli5: The ideas in this RFC were important and influenced later protocols, but CBT itself never became widely used. It is now considered historic, like an old-fashioned but well-designed system that was passed over for other things. However, people still study it to understand how multicast should work and the trade-offs between different approaches.
